lesson.title: The Gap Between the Symbol and the Part
lesson.summary: The resistor, capacitor, and inductor used in circuit equations are pure abstractions, while every real part also carries parasitic resistance, inductance, or capacitance that becomes impossible to ignore at high frequency or high precision.
lesson.body:
Circuit analysis up to this point has treated a resistor, capacitor, and inductor as pure, single purpose components: a resistor is only resistance, a capacitor is only capacitance, an inductor is only inductance, nothing else. That simplification is what makes the equations solvable, but no physical part manufactured from real materials is that pure. Every real component carries small amounts of the other two behaviors baked in as an unavoidable side effect of its physical construction.

A real resistor has a tiny parasitic inductance from the length of its leads or the geometry of its resistive element, and a tiny parasitic capacitance between its leads or turns, both usually negligible at low frequency but increasingly significant at radio frequencies. A real capacitor has an equivalent series resistance, called ESR, from losses in its electrodes and, in electrolytic types, its internal electrolyte, plus an equivalent series inductance, ESL, from its leads and internal plate structure, both effectively in series with the ideal capacitance. A real inductor has winding resistance, often called DCR, simply the resistance of the wire it is wound from, plus parasitic capacitance between adjacent turns, which together produce a self resonant frequency above which the part stops behaving like an inductor at all.

Worked example: a 100 microfarad electrolytic capacitor has an ESR of 0.5 ohms, a realistic value for that part type. At a frequency of 100 kilohertz, its ideal capacitive reactance is Xc = 1 divided by (2 pi f C) = 1 divided by (2 pi times 100000 times 0.0001). The denominator works out to 2 pi times 10, about 62.83, so Xc is about 0.0159 ohms. Comparing the two: the 0.5 ohm ESR is more than 30 times larger than the 0.0159 ohm ideal reactance at that frequency. In practice, this capacitor no longer behaves like a capacitor at 100 kilohertz at all, it behaves mostly like a 0.5 ohm resistor. This is precisely why real circuits pair a large electrolytic capacitor with a small ceramic capacitor in parallel for high frequency decoupling: ceramics have far lower ESR and ESL and stay genuinely capacitive to much higher frequencies.

These parasitics connect directly to earlier chapters. The heat generated by ESR under ripple current is exactly the kind of unwanted power dissipation that component power rating and derating exist to manage, separate from the capacitor's intended job of storing energy. And a capacitor's leads or an inductor's winding wire are, physically, ordinary conductors obeying the same R = rho L over A relationship covered under wire resistance, resistance that shows up as ESR and DCR respectively.

None of this makes the ideal component model wrong to use, it remains the right first pass for design intuition and hand calculation. But any circuit pushed to higher frequency, higher power, or higher precision eventually needs the fuller picture, usually supplied by a manufacturer's equivalent circuit model, where the pure symbol on the schematic gets a few extra elements added around it to match how the real part actually behaves.
